meta.titre: Excretory System: Nitrogenous Waste, Habitat and the Kidney
meta.sous_theme: Nitrogenous waste and the mammalian kidney

sections.contenu_markdown: A trader at Mboppi market in Douala sells live tilapia kept in a basin of water and also chickens in a cage. Both animals must get rid of the nitrogen from the proteins they digest, but they do it in very different ways. The type of waste an animal makes depends on its habitat and on how much water it can afford to lose. The GCE paper often tests this link, together with the work of the kidney in making urine and keeping the water balance of the blood.

items: Proteins are made of amino acids, which contain nitrogen.
Substances move across membranes by diffusion, osmosis and active transport.
The liver is the organ where many chemical reactions of metabolism occur.
The blood carries dissolved substances to the organs.

sections.titre: Excretion and nitrogenous waste in different habitats
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Excretion** is the removal from the body of the toxic or waste products of metabolism. Examples are carbon dioxide (lungs), urea (kidneys) and bile pigments (liver). It is different from **egestion**, which is the removal of undigested food that has never entered the body cells.

Excess amino acids cannot be stored. The liver **deaminates** them, removing the amino group as **ammonia**, and the remaining carbon skeleton is used in respiration. Ammonia is a toxic **nitrogenous waste**, and animals deal with it in one of three ways that depend on the **habitat** and the supply of water.

| Waste | Toxicity | Solubility | Water needed | Energy cost | Typical animals |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ammonia | Very toxic | Very soluble | Large volume to dilute it | None | Fresh water fish such as tilapia, tadpoles |
| Urea | Much less toxic | Soluble | Moderate | ATP used in the liver (ornithine cycle) | Mammals including humans, adult amphibians |
| Uric acid | Non-toxic | Almost insoluble | Very little; passed as a paste or crystals | Highest | Birds, insects, many reptiles |

The link with habitat is the key idea. Animals that live in **water** can lose ammonia by diffusion across the gills into the surrounding water, so no energy is spent converting it. Animals on **land** must save water, so they convert ammonia to urea, and animals in **dry, hot habitats** or that develop in a shelled egg convert it to uric acid, which can be stored as harmless crystals and lost with almost no water.

In mammals the main excretory organ is the **kidney**, which also regulates the water and salt content of the blood (osmoregulation).

variantes.nom: Why fresh water fish excrete ammonia
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to explain the type of waste in an aquatic habitat, or what happens when the water is polluted
variantes.contenu_markdown: Fresh water fish take in water by osmosis, so they have no need to save water and pass plenty of dilute urine. Ammonia diffuses out through the gills **down its concentration gradient** into the water. If the water contains a high concentration of ammonia, as in a crowded or stagnant pond, the gradient becomes small, ammonia builds up in the blood and the fish is poisoned. Making urea or uric acid would waste ATP for no benefit.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked how the kidney makes urine
variantes.contenu_markdown:
- **Ultrafiltration** in the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule: the afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent arteriole, so blood pressure is high. Water, glucose, amino acids, urea and ions pass through the fenestrated capillary wall, the basement membrane and the gaps between podocytes. Blood cells and large proteins stay in the blood.
- **Selective reabsorption** in the proximal convoluted tubule: all glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed by active transport and co-transport, together with about two thirds of the water and salts. The cells have microvilli and many mitochondria.
- **Loop of Henle**: the ascending limb pumps out salts, making the tissue fluid of the medulla very concentrated, so water can be drawn out of the descending limb and the collecting duct.
- **Distal tubule and collecting duct**: the final adjustment of water and salts. Urine contains water, urea and salts, but no glucose and no protein in a healthy person.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the water potential of the blood changes, for example after sweating or drinking
variantes.contenu_markdown: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect a fall in the water potential of the blood. The posterior pituitary releases **ADH**, which makes the collecting duct walls more permeable to water by inserting aquaporins. More water is reabsorbed, so a small volume of concentrated urine is produced. When blood water potential is high, less ADH is released and a large volume of dilute urine is produced. This is negative feedback.

sections.enonce_markdown: A healthy kidney pair produces glomerular filtrate at $125\ \mathrm{cm^3\,min^{-1}}$ and urine at $1\ \mathrm{cm^3\,min^{-1}}$. Calculate (i) the volume of filtrate formed in 24 hours in $\mathrm{dm^3}$, (ii) the volume of water reabsorbed in 24 hours and (iii) the percentage of the filtrate that is reabsorbed.

etapes.action: Find the daily volume of filtrate.
etapes.justification: There are 60 minutes in an hour and 24 hours in a day, so multiply the rate by $60\times24$.

etapes.action: Find the daily volume of urine.
etapes.justification: The same time factor applies to the urine rate.
What is not excreted as urine has been reabsorbed into the blood.
Percentage = part divided by whole times 100, with the filtrate as the whole.

sections.conclusion_markdown: About **$180\ \mathrm{dm^3}$** of filtrate is formed each day, **$178.6\ \mathrm{dm^3}$** is reabsorbed and **99.2%** of the filtrate returns to the blood; only about $1.4\ \mathrm{dm^3}$ leaves as urine.

items.erreur_markdown: Excretion is the removal of faeces from the body.
items.pourquoi_faux: Faeces consist mostly of undigested food that was never part of the body's metabolism, so its removal is egestion.
items.correction_markdown: Excretion is the **removal of metabolic waste** such as urea, carbon dioxide and bile pigments.

items.erreur_markdown: Birds excrete uric acid because it is more toxic and so is easier to remove.
items.pourquoi_faux: Uric acid is almost insoluble and non-toxic. It is lost with very little water, which is why it suits animals that must conserve water or that develop in a shelled egg.
items.correction_markdown: Uric acid is **insoluble and non-toxic**, so it saves water.

items.erreur_markdown: Fresh water fish make urea because they live in water that would dilute their blood.
items.pourquoi_faux: They already have plenty of water and can lose ammonia by diffusion through the gills, so converting it to urea would waste ATP.
items.correction_markdown: Fresh water fish excrete **ammonia** directly into the surrounding water.

items.erreur_markdown: Glucose is filtered out of the blood and lost in the urine.
items.pourquoi_faux: Glucose is filtered, but it is all reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule. Glucose in urine is a sign that the carriers are saturated, as in untreated diabetes mellitus.
items.correction_markdown: In a healthy person **all the glucose is reabsorbed**, so the urine contains none.

items.erreur_markdown: ADH makes the kidney produce more urine when the blood is too concentrated.
items.pourquoi_faux: ADH makes the collecting duct more permeable, so more water is reabsorbed and less urine is produced.
items.correction_markdown: High ADH gives **less, more concentrated urine**.

items.enonce_markdown:
Four animals are listed: a tilapia, a chicken, a cow and a lizard living in a dry rocky area.

(a) State the main nitrogenous waste of each animal.
(b) Give one reason for each answer that links the waste to the habitat of the animal.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Tilapia: **ammonia**. Chicken: **uric acid**. Cow: **urea**. Lizard in a dry area: **uric acid**.

(b) The tilapia lives in water, so ammonia diffuses out through the gills into the water and no ATP is wasted converting it. The chicken (a bird) develops in a shelled egg and conserves water, and insoluble uric acid can be stored harmlessly. The cow lives on land and needs to save some water, but has enough water to excrete soluble urea. The lizard in a dry habitat needs to lose as little water as possible, and uric acid is passed almost dry.

items.enonce_markdown:
The glomerular filtrate in a person is formed at $7.5\ \mathrm{dm^3}$ per hour and urine at $0.075\ \mathrm{dm^3}$ per hour. The concentration of urea is $0.30\ \mathrm{g\,dm^{-3}}$ in the filtrate and $20\ \mathrm{g\,dm^{-3}}$ in the urine.

(a) Calculate the percentage of the filtrate volume that is reabsorbed.
(b) By what factor is urea more concentrated in urine than in the filtrate?
(c) Calculate the mass of urea in $1.5\ \mathrm{dm^3}$ of this urine.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Volume reabsorbed $=7.5-0.075=7.425\ \mathrm{dm^3\,h^{-1}}$.

Percentage $=\dfrac{7.425}{7.5}\times100=$ **99.0%**.

(b) Factor $=\dfrac{20}{0.30}=66.7$, so urea is about **67 times more concentrated** in the urine. Water is reabsorbed while urea mostly stays in the tubule.

(c) Mass $=20\ \mathrm{g\,dm^{-3}}\times1.5\ \mathrm{dm^3}=$ **$30\ \mathrm{g}$**.

items.enonce_markdown:
A farmer works all day in the hot sun at Bamenda and drinks very little water.

(a) Describe the sequence of events that changes the volume and concentration of his urine.
(b) A urine test on another patient shows glucose, although the blood glucose level is not unusually high. Suggest an explanation based on the structure and function of the nephron.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Sweating lowers the volume of the blood plasma and so the water potential of the blood falls. **Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus** detect this and the **posterior pituitary** releases more **ADH**. ADH makes the walls of the distal tubule and collecting duct more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed by osmosis into the concentrated medulla. The result is a **small volume of concentrated urine**, which conserves water. When the water potential returns to normal, ADH release falls (negative feedback).

(b) Glucose is freely filtered and is normally all reabsorbed by carrier proteins in the proximal convoluted tubule. If the carrier proteins are damaged or too few (a low renal threshold), the glucose that is filtered cannot all be reabsorbed and the rest stays in the urine even though blood glucose is normal.

items_markdown: Excretion removes **metabolic waste**; egestion removes undigested food.
Excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver to form ammonia, which is converted to urea or uric acid in many animals.
**Ammonia** suits aquatic animals, **urea** suits most land animals, and **uric acid** suits animals that must save water or develop in a shelled egg.
The nephron makes urine by ultrafiltration, selective reabsorption, the loop of Henle and final adjustment in the collecting duct.
ADH increases the permeability of the collecting duct, so more water is reabsorbed and urine is more concentrated.
